item.description:
URL: https://pepsipu.com/blog/2026-10-switch2-jailbreak-ns2jb/, See on Hacker News

ns2jb is a software-only jailbreak of the switch 2 for the current latest firmware 23.0.1

Introduction

You can get a copy of the exploit from the ns2jb repository.

ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in fs sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.

To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in Dabney House who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.

Setup

The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:

Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.

The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.

That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.

Getting code execution

WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.

Code execution through the browser

It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.

We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc. Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.

Why?

  • WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.
  • Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.
  • And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.

Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed1, but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here2.

While that runs, let’s explore other options.

Code execution through smilehax2

My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:

  • They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1 does not support PAC.
  • Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.

Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this Discord RCE. I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.

In particular, I’m interested in SmileBASIC. This is because it’s been pwned before, in smilehax, giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.

Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked position + count <= array.length, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:

memmove(
    backing + position * 8,                  // start of the gap
    backing + (position + count) * 8,        // elements after the gap
    (length - position) * 8                  // bytes to copy
);

Say we have a string array R of length 4, and we run REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF. position + count wraps to 0x9fffffff. As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than array.length. The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32), pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an Out of memory error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.

This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the REMOVE, operations on R[0] will treat the array backing as if it were a string.

Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of R[0], the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of R[0].

This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.

Getting sysmodule RW

Okay, now we need to compromise a more privileged process. We’re interested in ordinary sysmodules and built-in sysmodules.

Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.

I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on audio and ldn. I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the NV service, probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?

The fs sysmodule

In the meantime, I started looking at the built-in fs sysmodule, because:

  • The Switch 1 code shows that it’s able to serve decrypted code.
  • There’s a lot of code.
  • It’s probably similar to the fs module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.

The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from fs, we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them. Other sysmodules like ldr and ro look enticing because they have permission to map executable memory3, but they don’t have large attack surfaces, especially from SmileBASIC. We’ll come back to them later.

Buffer overflow with path normalization

An IFileSystem handle has an IPC command, GetEntryType. This takes a path string, normalized with Path::Normalize.

Paths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like /..\, call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lol

We’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the BufferedStorage object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data. We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write4.

From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the saved PID to 1. Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.

Getting code execution as any ordinary sysmodule

Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is ro. All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The interface for the module seems pretty minimal too. It seemed more fruitful to pursue a logic bug than to look for memory corruption in ro directly.

Let’s revisit that first point about fs serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?

Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as Nintendo Content Archives, or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable, main, and program metadata, main.npdm.

To load a program, the built-in ldr sysmodule asks fs to open ExeFS, and fs replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem. fs also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:

  • Is Nintendo’s signature of main.npdm’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid?
  • Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?

Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:

  • the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;
  • the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;
  • the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;
  • the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;
  • those hashes fix the executable content.

In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the fs module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.

Arbitrary r/w to native code execution

Indeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer main.npdm for the loader’s first check, but the executable main itself can be arbitrary. The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem, fs has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.

There are two writes we perform:

  • The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original main.npdm and our replacement main.
  • The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent fs from crashing.

These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before fs processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?

The fs process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message, fs processes it. Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle fs waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when fs processes a loader message.

With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a main.npdm for!

Getting built-in sysmodule native code execution

What main.npdms do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s fsp-srv connection to copy the NPDM of any ordinary sysmodule or game.

We’ll use this capability to launch our own code using ro’s NPDM. As mentioned earlier, ro’s NPDM gives it permission to invoke kernel SVCs like SetProcessMemoryPermission, MapProcessCodeMemory, and MapProcessMemory. In this case, we’ll use MapProcessMemory to create a writeable view of fs’s existing code. We can also dump fs’s code by reading this view.

These calls, however, require a KProcess handle to the process. To get a handle to fs, we’ll use our ARW to overwrite IEventNotifier’s 4-byte handle with 0xffff8001 and then call GetEventHandle from SmileBASIC. The kernel interprets this value to mean “the current process’s handle”, so SmileBASIC gets fs’s KProcess handle.

We can then send this handle to our custom ro process, who patches fs’s code.

Conclusion

Arbitrary code execution with any ordinary sysmodule’s permissions seems really powerful. We can investigate hardware without first exploiting each device’s driver. I’m hopeful this will help the homebrew community make progress toward CFW.

In the short term, there are a few next steps I think would be interesting:

  • Porting the fs sysmodule exploit to WebKit. Now that we know what bug we want to exploit, being able to perform arbitrary IPC calls is not as valuable. We might be able to trigger ARW in fs by changing the data used by WebKit’s existing filesystem code.
  • This jailbreak is tethered, and we don’t currently have a way to compromise built-in sysmodules other than fs. fs is a built-in sysmodule, so SM skips service ACL checks from fs, providing the same capabilities as smhax. I wonder if we can find bugs in other built-in modules?
  • With native code execution in fs, we can orchestrate its crypto hardware directly. For example, it’s used for NCA4 decryption.
  • The exploit has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven’t gotten around to packaging it yet. It wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip, but it wouldn’t require any external hardware.

For now, I’m excited to see all the upcoming Switch 2 homebrew, emulation, and modding.

  1. It did not succeed. ↩

  2. It’s not inherently bad to attempt a WebKit exploit. Once we have a bug in a sysmodule we know to be valuable, it might make sense to go back and try to exploit it in WebKit with a data-only attack. This is because WebKit is accessible offline, meaning Nintendo can’t withdraw it like an eShop title. However, at this stage of our research, it’s not worth the cost to our iteration speed. ↩

  3. I wonder if one day Nintendo will map ordinary sysmodules and even game code via encrypted blobs only the kernel or secure monitor can decrypt. Then, no userspace process could observe any code on the system—there can never be RX mappings in userspace. Even the loader module, which starts new processes, would ask a higher exception level to load encrypted blobs it supplies. There’d be tradeoffs, like games being unable to read their own code at runtime. However, Nintendo has already started removing dynamic code features, like the JIT sysmodule. I wonder if this is the direction the Switch is headed. Luckily, that day is not today. ↩

  4. Initially, Codex’s read/write primitive repeated the buffer overflow on the cache object each time it wanted to change the backing buffer pointer. This hurts stability, especially when following many pointers consecutively, since each change is a chance to crash the system. We can use a similar trick to the one here. We can use some overflows to point the first cache entry’s backing buffer pointer at another cache entry’s metadata. Then we can replace the second cache entry’s pointer without risking more overflows. ↩

item.title: OpenAI CLI (208 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/openai/openai-cli, See on Hacker News

The official CLI for the OpenAI REST API.

Installation

Installing with Homebrew

brew install openai/tools/openai

Installing with Go

To test or install the CLI locally, you need Go version 1.26 or later installed.

go install 'github.com/openai/openai-cli/cmd/openai@latest'

Once you have run go install, the binary is placed in your Go bin directory:

  • Default location: $HOME/go/bin (or $GOPATH/bin if GOPATH is set)
  • Check your path: Run go env GOPATH to see the base directory

If commands aren't found after installation, add the Go bin directory to your PATH:

# Add to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, etc.)
export PATH="$PATH:$(go env GOPATH)/bin"

The first eligible interactive openai run quietly saves image picker Tab shortcuts for future Bash, zsh, and fish sessions. Open a new terminal to use them. See shortcut setup and removal for requirements and opt-out. PowerShell keeps normal Tab completion; press Enter after openai images generate to open the picker.

Update notices

Bare openai checks for newer stable releases when stdin, stdout, and stderr are terminals. It adds a plain-text notice below help, at most once every seven days. Explicit help, commands, completion, CI, and redirected streams skip the check entirely.

The notice includes an update command when the CLI can verify its installation method. Verified Homebrew installations use brew upgrade --cask openai/tools/openai. Go commands require a verified binary, an available Go command, and an explicit matching GOBIN. Custom GOOS or GOARCH settings select the installation guide instead. Go upgrades to major version 2 or later also select the installation guide. Unknown installations receive the installation-guide link instead. The CLI never installs updates automatically.

Checks use public GitHub release metadata without API credentials, at most once daily. Checks respect HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY, including their lowercase forms. Update discovery waits at most 200 milliseconds. Failed checks remain silent. Package-manager availability can lag a new GitHub release. Set OPENAI_CLI_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to disable checks and notices.

Running Locally

After cloning the git repository for this project, you can use the scripts/run script to run the tool locally:

Usage

The CLI follows a resource-based command structure:

openai <resource> [subresource...] <command> [flags...]

Standard API endpoints require an API key:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

openai responses create \
  --input "Say this is a test" \
  --model gpt-5.5

Admin endpoints require an admin API key:

export OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY="sk-admin-..."

openai admin organization usage completions \
  --start-time 1735689600 \
  --end-time 1735776000 \
  --bucket-width 1d

Browse each group with --help, for example openai admin --help or openai admin organization --help. Existing colon commands such as openai admin:organization:usage completions continue to work.

Run openai to browse command groups by task, with descriptions for each group. Group help separates actions from nested command groups and lists every immediate command. Help works without an API key or network connection:

openai help setup                  # Enter your API key safely
openai images generate --help      # Example and every image option
openai help images generate        # The same complete image help
openai --help                      # Command groups and global options

Add --help (or -h) to any command for its complete help page. openai help COMMAND shows the same page. Command pages list global options. Use openai --help for their full descriptions. You can place --help after valid command options. The old help --all spelling prints migration guidance and the complete page. Command behavior, defaults, and output formats remain unchanged. Tab completion follows the same group order and supports help topics and file input paths. After upgrading, reload shell completion to enable the new file-path behavior. Older loaded completion scripts keep their previous behavior until refreshed.

Enable command insertion to fill your command line from examples, setup guidance, and recovery commands. Ctrl+X, then Tab searches suggestions without running them. Double Tab is an optional binding for Bash, zsh, and fish.

Successful JSON responses print readable text by default, including in pipes. Use --format json or --format jsonl in scripts that parse API data. See reading command results for extraction, binary output, and the scope of readable presentation.

Upload a local file with an explicit purpose, inspect its metadata, then download its contents:

openai files upload "upload space.txt" --purpose user_data
openai files get file-example
openai files download file-example --output "downloaded copy.txt"
openai files download file-example > copy.txt

Replace file-example with the returned file ID. Upload takes a plain path, without an added @. create, retrieve, content, and their existing flags remain available. See working with files for literal filenames, output formats, and script examples.

openai images generate --prompt "A tiny orange robot" saves images to ~/Downloads/gpt-images/ and prints their paths, including in pipes. The CLI uses gpt-image-2.5-sunburst when saving without an explicit model or legacy response format. Use --model for another exact ID, --name for a filename, or --output-dir for an existing directory. Existing files are kept. --format json returns API data without saving or applying the CLI preset. images edit also saves new results while keeping source files. images create-variation is retired and no longer available. To create a variation, use images edit with a GPT Image model and a prompt. See image generation and saving for commands and defaults.

openai images preview "path/to/image.png" redisplays a saved image without an API request. Use openai images inline on or off to remember whether future saved images appear automatically. Per-command --inline auto, on or off overrides that setting. on also permits an image font in local Apple Terminal.

Errors print actionable summaries to stderr by default. Use --format-error json for original API error details, including unknown fields and SDK-reported stream error events. For those events, extraction paths include the error envelope, for example --transform-error error.code. Explicit --format values json, jsonl, raw, and yaml also apply to errors unless overridden by --format-error; an explicit --format-error auto or text restores summaries. --transform-error extracts error data independently of successful output. Malformed or empty error bodies receive a safe diagnostic; HTTP status is included only when the SDK retains it. Summaries omit rejected values and request URLs; explicit API error details can contain server-supplied sensitive data.

Environment variables

Environment variable Required Default value
OPENAI_API_KEY no null
OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY no null
OPENAI_ORG_ID no null
OPENAI_PROJECT_ID no null
OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET no null
OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS no null
OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE no null
OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE no null
OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN no false

Global flags

  • --api-key (can also be set with OPENAI_API_KEY env var)
  • --admin-api-key (can also be set with OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY env var)
  • --organization (can also be set with OPENAI_ORG_ID env var)
  • --project (can also be set with OPENAI_PROJECT_ID env var)
  • --webhook-secret (can also be set with OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET env var)
  • --mtls-client-cert-file (can also be set with OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE env var)
  • --mtls-client-key-file (can also be set with OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE env var)
  • --help - Show command line usage
  • --debug - Enable debug logging. This includes HTTP request/response details and bodies; do not share debug logs if they may contain sensitive payloads.
  • --version, -v - Show the CLI version
  • --base-url - Use a custom API backend URL. HTTPS is required except for localhost or literal loopback IP addresses such as 127.0.0.1 and ::1. This also applies to OPENAI_BASE_URL; remote HTTP backends must enable HTTPS.
  • --header, -H - Add a literal request header as Name: Value; repeat for multiple headers
  • --format - Change the output format (auto, text, explore, json, jsonl, pretty, raw, yaml); auto selects readable text unless extracting data
  • --format-error - Change the stderr error format (auto, text, explore, json, jsonl, pretty, raw, yaml); auto selects readable summaries unless extracting error data
  • --transform - Transform the data output using GJSON syntax
  • --transform-error - Transform the error output using GJSON syntax

Request headers

Use --header or -H before or after a resource command:

openai --header 'X-Trace-ID: example-123' models list \
  -H 'X-Client-Label: local,manual'

Values are literal: commas and colons are preserved, and @ prefixes do not read files. Surrounding spaces and tabs are trimmed from values. -H 'X-Example:' sends an empty value. If a name is repeated, the last value wins regardless of case, overriding default and endpoint-specific headers. Headers managed by the HTTP transport, such as Host and Content-Length, retain the transport's behavior. Supplied header values are hidden in help and redacted in debug logs.

For credential-bearing headers, have a secret manager or trusted launcher set OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS directly in the CLI's environment. This keeps credentials out of command arguments and avoids typing literal secrets into shell history. The variable accepts one Name: Value entry per line. For example, with non-sensitive values:

export OPENAI_CUSTOM_HEADERS='X-Trace-ID: example-123
X-Client-Label: local,manual'
openai models list

--header and endpoint-specific header flags override matching environment entries. Environment header values are also redacted in debug logs. Use OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY for standard API and admin authentication.

Mutual TLS

Mutual TLS is currently in beta. To opt in and activate a CA certificate for your organization or project, follow the OpenAI Mutual TLS Beta Program instructions.

To authenticate API-key requests with a mutual TLS client certificate, provide the client certificate and private key as separate PEM files. If certificate chain support is enabled for your organization, the certificate file must contain the leaf certificate first, followed by any intermediate certificates. Otherwise, use a client certificate signed directly by an activated CA certificate.

export OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_FILE=/run/secrets/openai/client-chain.pem
export OPENAI_MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/openai/client.key
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://mtls.api.openai.com/v1

openai files list

Both mTLS files must be configured together. Keep the private key in a permission-restricted file; do not put private-key contents directly in command arguments or environment variables. The CLI does not automatically select an mTLS endpoint, so configure OPENAI_BASE_URL or --base-url explicitly. HTTP and SOCKS proxies remain supported, but HTTPS proxies are rejected to prevent presenting the client certificate during the proxy's own TLS handshake.

Passing files as arguments

For JSON input values, @myfile.ext reads local file contents:

Binary upload flags use plain paths. For example, use files upload --file "upload space.txt" --purpose user_data. Here, --file "@upload space.txt" names an actual file starting with @; it does not expand another file reference. See working with files.

openai <command> --arg @abe.jpg

Files can also be passed inside JSON or YAML blobs:

openai <command> --arg '{image: "@abe.jpg"}'
# Equivalent:
openai <command> <<YAML
arg:
  image: "@abe.jpg"
YAML

When piping JSON or YAML from an untrusted source, enable untrusted-stdin mode:

untrusted-producer | OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN=1 openai <command> --file ./upload.txt

In this mode, values supplied through stdin are treated as literal data: @, @file://, and @data:// references in request bodies, headers, and query parameters do not read local files. File-upload parameters must be provided explicitly as command-line flags. Explicit flags retain their normal file behavior and take precedence over values supplied through stdin. Leave OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN unset when using trusted heredocs or other trusted piped input that intentionally references local files.

If you need to pass a string literal that begins with an @ sign, you can escape the @ sign to avoid accidentally passing a file.

openai <command> --username '\@abe'

Explicit encoding

For JSON endpoints, the CLI tool does filetype sniffing to determine whether the file contents should be sent as a string literal (for plain text files) or as a base64-encoded string literal (for binary files). If you need to explicitly send the file as either plain text or base64-encoded data, you can use @file://myfile.txt (for string encoding) or @data://myfile.dat (for base64-encoding). Note that absolute paths will begin with @file:// or @data://, followed by a third / (for example, @file:///tmp/file.txt).

openai <command> --arg @data://file.txt

Linking different Go SDK versions

You can link the CLI against a different version of the OpenAI Go SDK for development purposes using the ./scripts/link script.

To link to a specific version from a repository (version can be a branch, git tag, or commit hash):

./scripts/link github.com/org/repo@version

To link to a local copy of the SDK:

./scripts/link ../path/to/openai-go

If you run the link script without any arguments, it will default to ../openai-go.

Contributing

Please share bug reports and feature requests through GitHub issues. Pull requests are limited to repository collaborators; we do not accept pull requests from non-collaborators. See CONTRIBUTING.md for the contribution policy and development guide. For security vulnerabilities, follow SECURITY.md.

item.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal (414 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/, See on Hacker News

TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videos

How it sees a terminal

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell.1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

A session

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

BOS SCREEN_START 32 96
ROW_0 0 'simedw@laptop:~$ '
CURSOR 0 17 1
SCREEN_END

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r, Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.

INPUT_START 'l' INPUT_END

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

OUTPUT_START
ROW_0 17 'l'
CURSOR 0 18 1
OUTPUT_END

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l, then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

Copying rows

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

So I added a COPY operation instead:

ROW_0 COPY 1
ROW_1 COPY 2  
ROW_2 COPY 3
...

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.

Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.

That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.

Generating the training data

I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.

Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own.

The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one.

The synthetic recipe was:

  1. Randomize usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, terminal sizes.
  2. Randomize directories and files based on a fictional persona (developer, sysadmin, etc.).
  3. Pick 6–24 weighted activities (modify files, vim, python, tmux, etc.).
  4. Track state, so sessions mostly open files that exist.
  5. Type like a person: one keypress at a time, with tab completion etc. I set the typo rate to 1.2%, which is generous to me.
  6. 35% of sessions start partway through, forcing the model to learn to work from any state.

The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.

I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.

Training

I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage.

I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.

Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves.

In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.

Learning from its own mistakes

To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations.2

For each training example:

  1. Pick a point in a recorded session, usually close to the command that produces the output.
  2. Let the model predict the next 1-4 events.
  3. Compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen.
  4. If the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress.
  5. Continue training on the corrected frame and a few subsequent real events.

The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.

There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.

For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.

Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.

About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.

Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.

In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.

Testing

I use three tests. ShellBench has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. PresetBench has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.

The memory test has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training.3

How much does fine-tuning help?

Model4 ShellBench /106 File readbacks /13
Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, prompted 52 2
Qwen3-0.6B, prompted 60 3
WorldTUI 80 9

The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.

It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after echo green >> colors, running cat colors often doesn't show the appended line.

Making it fast

For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.

But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen (vim test.txt, man, clear) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.

Rows in parallel

What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.

That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.

The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.

This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.

Rows that can't talk to each other

This might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to vim opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.

The solution was speculative decoding.

Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.

Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.

The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft.

In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like man test takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification.5

Making it smaller

I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens,6 so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB).

I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB.

The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab.

Distilling

Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output.

My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens.

That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory.

In the end I gave up on distilling it.

What it can do

Memory

This was the part I was most interested in. Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged.

The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with cat, I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive!

Other applications

It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux.

In vim, it handles the mode switch on esc and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode.

What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model.

It even manages environment variables and variable expansion.

Python

Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: pythoon launches Python, but ython doesn't.

What doesn't work

I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring. Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations.

Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path. There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency.

In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause.

As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it.

Back in 2022, people were already prompting ChatGPT to act as a Linux terminal. More recently, GameNGen simulated Doom using diffusion, and NeuralOS tackled a desktop GUI.

WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux.

Summary

I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected.

What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath.

It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding.

One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues.

Try it here. It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find.

I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here.

item.title: Airbnb bans making guests do dishes and take out the trash (221 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theverge.com/tech/1015844/airbnb-chores-house-rules-update, See on Hacker News

Stevie Bonifield

is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Checking out of your next Airbnb might be less of a hassle now that the company is banning hosts from including time-consuming chores in their house rules. Airbnb’s updated house rules policy, which starts with reservations booked on or after November 20th, says hosts can’t ask guests to “complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner.” According to Airbnb, that includes:

  • Dishes: Guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes, but you can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
  • Laundry: Guests shouldn’t be asked to remove sheets from the bed or start a load of laundry, but you can ask them to gather used towels.
  • Trash: Guests shouldn’t be asked to take garbage off-site, but you can ask them to separate their trash and recycling into designated indoor bins.
  • Utilities: Guests shouldn’t be asked to avoid using a listed amenity like air conditioning, but you can ask them to turn it off when they leave.

Airbnb is displaying hosts’ requests more prominently now in a new “rules and requests” section on listings. You might see an “includes cleaning requests” warning if a host leaves chore requests in their listing after the new policy goes into effect. Hosts aren’t allowed to sneak in extra rules in messages to guests or on signs around their property, either.

Some hosts pushed back on the house rules restrictions on Airbnb’s forums, saying they pose health risks and arguing that guests can simply choose not to stay at listings with overly-strict rules. Airbnb says there can be exceptions to the limits on checkout chores, like asking guests to “dispose of trash in an animal-proof container in bear country.”

item.title: There isn't an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability (594 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://eliastaylor.com/noexploit/, See on Hacker News

I know, I know. It's all you're hearing about. That, and the number 4.

Don't get me wrong, there's clearly a bug here and it really does matter. But this is not easy to exploit. It is certainly nowhere near as eay as Log4Shell/Heartbleed/RoRYaml etc.

Justify yourself, you lunatic!

I don't think this PHP vulnerability is that exploitable. I think that 5 years ago people would've understood this, but now people are being deluded by their LLMs telling them they have an exploit when they don't.

If you take a look at github right now, there are thousands, literally thousands, of "PoC" exploits for this vulnerability. One thing you'll notice about all of them though, is that they do not work against a vanilla PHP instance.

Go ahead, stand up a php server you think is vulnerable in Docker and then run the PoC yourself. Don't get your LLM to do it. No. Run the script, yourself. The exploits don't work.

Where's the exploit, Lebowski?

I think that a lot of people had assumed that LLMs will be able to build an exploit chain instantly from reading the diff, and that even if this was harder to exploit than other exploits, LLMs would've levelled the playing field. Well. There's no working exploit. Now what?

When I think about "we're very fucked" CVE10s on the Internet, I think of the following vulnerabilities:

  • RoR YAML decoding (send a post body with bad yaml in it)
  • Log4shell (set your user-agent to ${jdni:ldap:})
  • Shellshock ("copy env x='() { :;}; echo vulnerable' bash -c "echo this is a test"" and edit to taste)
  • Heartbleed (ask for Content-Length 10000000)

The second these vulnerabilities made the news, there were botnets doing the rounds causing damage. And this was before LLMs! People have to write the botnets. With their hands!

It's been 10 hours since this vulnerability has been posted, and half the software world is looking at it, and lord knows 100,000 people have got their "superintelligence" on the case. Nevertheless, there's no working exploit. The ones doing the rounds are fake, or only work in a lab, because...

Fucking LLMs, man.

Script kiddies (and script adults, who have also switched their brains off) now all think that, well, they don't understand UAF chaining, but this Claude guy knows everything and can totally make an exploit.

Hilariously, this results in the LLM giving their younger-brother an unplugged controller. It says exploit all across the screen... and has some smoking gun transcripts... but it's modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability. Cheating!!

  • https://github.com/david-alvarez-rosa/php-rce
  • https://github.com/eness/php2shell-CVE-2026-109618-CVE-2026-109619-PoC
  • https://github.com/ikow/php2shell-poc

One really amusing thing in common with most of these "PoC"s is that they lean on "LFI", or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability. In non-php terms, their exploit chain requires the server to effectively do eval(read(filename_provided_by_user)).

It's not rare for PHP apps to be fucked in some sense, but requiring the server to have an existing vulnerability where one could cat /etc/password is an insane pre-requisite. If you need this, this does not make this a severe bug.

The strangest thing is that so many people have independently made this extraordinarily weird defect in judgement. That is because they haven't independently made this decision. Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them, hence the bizarre distribution in logical errors.

There's something important to be said here about how many people have Claude/GPT make design decisions for them, and how AI is the primary decision maker in the world right now. You've got this bizarre case of "Decision Schelling Points" where a method of solving a problem is extremely overrepresented, because it's what Claude does out of the box.

This is annoying in the case of "most websites look the same now", but because LLMs have the power to ruin every domain at the same time, this is also "most decisions are suspiciously the same now". Especially in this case, where AI is inserting a vulnerability on the server... to prove that the server is vulnerable to your "exploit any PHP instance" attack!

So why was everyone so scared?

Because:

  1. A PHP core team member said that this was cataclysmic ("exploits will start appearing 15 minutes after the patch drops")
  2. We all deep down know that PHP is insecure
  3. The exploit video had an anime girl in it
  4. We all know that LLMs are looming over the internet like a 100 ton chekov's anvil, and we know that code isn't secure

And we've had things like this before, but not in the LLM era yet. Luckily for us, this doesn't seem to be that day. This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment.

item.description:
URL: https://blog.railway.com/p/security-disclosure-wednesday-october-21st, See on Hacker News

Earlier this morning, Railway detected anomalous activity involving systems that store customer environment variables. After further investigation, our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.

We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers. We have notified these upstream providers to revoke all keys proactively, as we take these kinds of events extremely seriously.

While our initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, we are nevertheless recommending that all users take the actions described below as a precaution to protect your systems while we complete our review.

item.title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military (124 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmreyvepnv0po, See on Hacker News

Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use.

The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts.

Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so.

"Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity.

In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles."

"We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind."

But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight.

After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said.

Those values, according to Google's AI Principles, include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments.

The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for.

Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns.

Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future."

"Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added.

In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities.

The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data.

Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up.

Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation."

However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year.

Google's contract with the Pentagon, which was signed earlier this year, allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control".

Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations.

As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war.

"AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team.

"When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors."

Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company.

"In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising".

Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak."

A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave – but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard."

Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]."

"Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said.

Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services".

Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.

Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch believes AI technology in warfare is not ready for the battlefield. "Current AI models are not robust enough, and I don't think they have been trained for such tasks either," he said.

Additional reporting by Rosa Rahimi

      • Apply #[non_exhaustive] to public structs with public fields
      • #[must_use] on functions
      • #[must_use] on types

    • Implementation concerns
      • Don’t overuse type inference
